For example, a verified booking screen shows that the UI reflects a date change, but does not inherently prove that airline system databases successfully processed a refund or cancellation ticket. TaskVM’s live state projection surfaces exactly what the system can observe, flagging when visual evidence is insufficient rather than silently assuming consistency. This transparency highlights that interface trust should be grounded in explicit model boundaries, not in exaggerated claims of system-wide correctness.

8.4. Designing for Bounded Recovery and Irreversibility

A prevalent tendency in automated agent design is the masking of failures through optimistic self-reporting. When an agent makes an irreversible error, such as deleting a contact record, conversational interfaces often provide vague reassurances, misleading users into believing the action can be undone. TaskVM implements a tripartite taxonomy of reversibility. Reversible and compensatable actions are tracked and counteracted through inverse GUI gestures, while irreversible operations are explicitly locked to prevent deceptive undo representations. Empirically, participants exercised goal interventions in every task by design, and 11 of 37 additionally invoked rollback a total of 17 times under TaskVM (baseline: 2 participants, 4 times), with 13 of those 17 events occurring outside the two tasks that scripted an undo request, demonstrating that participants reached for the exposed recovery control even when not asked to.

We note that compensating actions, such as sending a cancellation message, do not equate to true atomic rollbacks. They introduce secondary effects and may leave behind specific audit trails in third-party systems. By forcing the interface to distinguish between these recovery modes, TaskVM shifts user trust away from fictional comprehensive undo capabilities toward calibrated expectations about what can, and cannot, be reversed.

Our evidence also reveals a productive tension: rollback is simultaneously the most demanded governance capability and the hardest to make reliable. Rollback was the operation our baselines lacked entirely, the function 11 of 37 study participants invoked (17 events) beyond scripted requests, and the automation Stage 3 participants requested in stronger form, asking for checkpoints placed automatically at failure-prone nodes. Yet the one unresolved failure in our stress tier is precisely a rollback-compensation family, blocked by a race between a signing window and the confirmation gesture. We read this convergence not as a defect to be excused but as the clearest roadmap the paradigm offers: honest vocabulary about recovery creates demand for reliable recovery, and the engineering agenda should follow the demand.

9. Limitations and Future Work

Our results are bounded in several ways. Stage 2 holds the environment and the replayed agent trajectory constant, which isolates perception but cannot evidence live-model execution success or real recovery capability; its read probes reached only a subset of trials (n=8n=8 matched pairs), so probe accuracy is directional evidence rather than an established gain in understanding. Stage 3 restores a live model and participant-authored tasks but removes the control arm, so its lower workload is descriptive and confounded with task freedom and practice, and its sample is self-selected: the 14 returning participants had shown a substantially larger Stage 2 workload advantage than the 23 who did not return (−24.70-24.70 versus +0.14+0.14 NASA-TLX points). Participants were recruited from a single laboratory research-volunteer pool skewing toward university students and researchers. All stages ran on an offline simulated application suite with finite injected data, so open-ended search occasionally missed the corpus, adding noise without affecting the governance mechanism; cross-platform deployment is engineering-supported through our substrate adapters but not empirically demonstrated here; live-model execution failures such as retry loops originate in the executor layer, yet their consequences still require an interface that can surface and govern them. On the system side, our compiled schemas express structured productivity workflows whose state maps to discrete variables and invariant predicates; continuous creative workflows (video editing, 3D modeling, freehand illustration) resist this decomposition, and our purely visual polling can miss sub-second transient UI states, complicating fine-grained causal diagnosis. Finally, TaskVM deliberately does not circumvent defensive gates such as CAPTCHAs; graceful human handoff at such boundaries, broader and more diverse samples, production substrates, and equivalence-controlled live-model comparisons are the natural next steps.

10. Conclusion

As autonomous agents gain the ability to execute complex workflows, the object users must govern is not the agent’s procedure but the state of the world the agent touches. We present task-state governance, an interaction model that frames a cross-application task as an editable relationship among desired outcomes, protected facts, and observed application state. TaskVM instantiates this relationship through task-level controls, separately checked observations, and explicitly bounded recovery.

Our evaluation characterizes three distinct questions with three distinct designs: technical capability and cost on a fixed benchmark suite, subjective experience under controlled replay, and exploratory use by returning participants on self-authored tasks. These are complementary forms of evidence rather than three confirmations of one mechanism, and each carries the boundaries registered in the preceding section. Together they show that the obligations and limits of agent-mediated change can be made explicit objects of interaction, verifiable in principle and inspectable in use, while live-execution effectiveness and broader generalization remain open to further study. By shifting the unit of interaction from procedural plans to verifiable state contracts, TaskVM suggests how users can govern autonomous agents with clarity and calibrated trust: humans govern tasks, while agents operate applications.

Data Availability

Analysis scripts and de-identified aggregate data will be released with the supplementary materials. Identity mappings and raw screen recordings are withheld to protect participant privacy.

Appendix A Contract-Outcome Verification Predicates

This appendix defines the ten Contract-Outcome Verification (COV) predicates used to adjudicate every Stage 1 trial. Each trial is scored on every applicable predicate; a strict pass requires all applicable predicates to pass.

Appendix B Stage 1 Data Quality Notes

We document the exclusion and correction decisions behind the Stage 1 numbers so the reported tables can be audited cell by cell.

Five trials in the first wave failed at the infrastructure level rather than at task execution (two vendor server errors and three setup timeouts); these were re-run cleanly, and their invalidated records were removed from all denominators. Two further trials misclassified by the fail-loud grading gate (one true pass and one valid failure) were vindicated in a subsequent envelope audit and counted correctly. Frozen pass verdicts are regression-locked and can never be reversed by later waves. In the skills-ON wave, TaskVM has valid cells for 23 of 36 instances; the remaining cells are recorded as missing rather than scored as failures, and a cell-level index cross-validation across all 108 cells reported zero mismatches.

The skills-ON wave initially produced a misleading side artifact: a cell-level index in which all baseline cells were marked as failures due to a residual obsolete progress gate. The authoritative rollup supersedes that index (Direct-CUA 19/36, Planner-CUA 18/36); any aggregation from the raw cells would reproduce the obsolete gate and is excluded by an on-record erratum.

Finally, the non-inferiority analysis reported in Table 3 is the corrected protocol version computed after adjudication of the frozen waves. An earlier draft compared the skills-ON and skills-OFF waves against each other and was inconclusive; the corrected analysis follows the evaluation protocol in comparing TaskVM against its strongest baseline within a single wave on contract-faithful execution, pairing 35 task clusters and resampling 10,000 times with a fixed seed. At the 10 percentage-point margin specified in our evaluation protocol the one-sided 95 percent lower bound (−0.0857-0.0857) clears the margin, establishing non-inferiority; sensitivity analyses at 5 and 7.5 points remain inconclusive, and the verdict also holds at 15 points. The 23-of-36 valid strict-COV cells and the 35 CFE clusters are explicitly different analysis collections: the former retains only fully measured cells, whereas the latter additionally admits the protocol’s per-family fallback judgments, so the larger CFE count does not contradict the smaller COV count, and the 35 clusters are instance-level pairings between TaskVM and Direct-CUA, not a separate task set.

Appendix C Comparison with Prior Systems

This appendix positions TaskVM among representative interactive agent systems along one organizing axis: the primary object each interface asks the user to govern. For each system we trace the consequences of that choice, namely what a user edit commits the system to, what counts as completion, and what recovery can mean. These are differences in kind, not rankings: the rows are not benchmarked under a shared protocol, and each cell characterizes the system as presented by its authors; where a column falls outside a system’s reported model, we mark it as such rather than implying incapability.

Appendix D Stage 2 Interface Conditions

The two interface conditions compared in Stage 2 are shown separately below. In the baseline Conversational CUA condition (Figure 7), participants supervise an agent through an application screencast accompanied by an interactive chat drawer. In the TaskVM condition (Figure 7), participants govern execution through the governance cockpit with the live application view beside the editable task-state controls.

Appendix E Per-Family COV Outcomes

Figure 8 reports the strict COV pass rate for every task family in the frozen benchmark suite. Aggregate condition-level rates are the primary comparison (Figure 4); per-family rates are noisy by construction, since each cell aggregates only a handful of trials, and are reported here for completeness and auditability.

Appendix F Stage 1 Per-Instance Outcomes

Table 8 lists the strict COV verdict of every frozen instance in the skills-OFF main wave, so that the aggregate rates in Table 1 can be audited cell by cell. A ✓ means every applicable predicate passed on that instance’s trial (Section A). The Template Control column is omitted: it is an invalid sanity-check harness rather than a baseline (Section B); its per-instance record is preserved in the frozen data. All four families in which no condition passed (cav, irv, and rbv variants rbv-02/03) are retained; no failing family is hidden.

Appendix G Stage 2 Task Battery and Mid-Task Events

Table 9 specifies the full Stage 2 battery: four counterbalanced task pairs, each pair sharing one governance archetype across two surfaces. The mid-task event was delivered by the experimenter at the trigger point shown, under the wizard-of-Oz replay protocol; the same event sequence, timing, and error manifestations were replayed in both interface conditions. Each participant completed three of the eight tasks per condition; read/write probes were assigned to task slots by a deterministic balanced schedule (per-arm probe types per participant are recorded in the session logs). All contact names are fictional entities of the offline simulator.

Appendix H Stage 3 Usage in Aggregate

To protect participant privacy, the anonymized archive retains per-episode runtime counters (goal formulation, status, model-call count) rather than complete GUI interaction traces, and some open-ended search terms typed by participants are withheld entirely. We therefore report Stage 3 usage in aggregate (Table 10) instead of as per-task transcripts, and point readers to the open-ended responses (Table 11) for what participants themselves chose to disclose about their tasks. Per-episode success is not adjudicated (Stage 3 embedded no probes and no per-task ground truth). Model calls are the LLM invocations attributed to an episode by the runtime ledger; application and contact names appearing anywhere in the study are fictional entities of the offline simulator.

Diversity is visible at the aggregate level. The fourteen participants differ markedly in how they used the open session: total model calls span 3 to 149 per participant (median 52.5), episodes span 1 to 4 (median 3), and tasks touched five distinct application surfaces across the cohort (messaging: 11 participants; social feed: 7; video platform: 4; music: 3; content community: 2). An independence audit confirmed that no two participants produced an identical episode sequence: even where two participants issued a textually identical goal, the runs differ in status, timing, and model-call counts (e.g., 3, 41, 46, 50, 63, and 73 calls on six runs of one shared formulation).

Appendix I Stage 3 Open-Ended Response Evidence Map

Table 11 maps every theme reported in Section 7 to its supporting participants and a representative verbatim quote. Themes were coded by the research team from the two open-ended questionnaire items; frequencies count distinct participants, a participant may contribute to several themes, and quotes are translated from the Chinese originals with the participant ID preserved. We report open-ended responses, not interviews; no inter-rater reliability is claimed.

Appendix J Stage 3 Participant-Submitted Screenshots

Figures 9 and 10 were spontaneously captured and voluntarily submitted to the research team by two Stage 3 participants. The interface language of the study deployment is Chinese; both images are reproduced without any modification or translation.

Appendix K Stage 2 Measurement Instruments

Table 12 reproduces every item of the condition-end questionnaire administered once per condition (instrument condition_end_v1, Chinese administration with officially paired English strings; English shown verbatim). Composites: NASA-TLX = unweighted mean of the six 0–100 sliders (the performance slider runs Perfect →\to Failure, so all dimensions share the demand direction); UMUX-Lite = mean⁡(items−1)/6×100\mathrm{mean}(\mathrm{items}-1)/6\times 100; recovery control = mean of the four rc_* items; trust = mean of tia_trust and tia_rely; perceived transparency = mean of the three predictability items with tia_unpredictable_R reverse-scored (8−raw8-\mathrm{raw}); support satisfaction = mean of the three asq_* items. All Likert items used 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). The post-study background questionnaire (Appendix M) is a separate instrument.

Read probes were embedded in drift-triggered trials: three multiple-choice questions per probe covering committed effects, the effective goal, and governance facts, drawn from a frozen probe bank (per-task options and answer keys frozen before data collection; scoring = exact key match per question), preceded by a single 0–100 confidence rating for the whole probe. Write probes scored the participant’s own intervention at the scripting boundary and at trial end against the frozen expectation for that task (both endpoints recorded per participant per arm).

Appendix L Evaluation Configuration

In all stages the user-facing runtime observes only rendered pixels and emits standard GUI gestures; oracle-only capabilities (state resets, internal-state reads, deterministic event injection) are confined to an isolated evaluation harness and are never exposed to the interactive session, as detailed in the prototype section. Per-trial manifests record model identity, per-role call counts, and wall time; frozen artifacts per instance are retained in the consolidated archive cited in Section 5.

Appendix M Participant Demographics and Background

M.1. What was collected, and from whom

Demographic and background information was collected after the main study through two voluntary channels. (i) At compensation time, participants could provide identifying contact information together with self-reported gender, age, and affiliation; 36 of the 37 completers did so, and one (P08) declined all background collection. (ii) On 2026-09-12 we additionally administered a five-item background questionnaire (field of study; professional background related to AI agents; usage frequency of three classes of AI systems; AI products used; purposes of use) as a web page gated by roster name verification; 35 of the 37 completers answered it, one (P32) submitted compensation information but declined the questionnaire. The questionnaire was administered in Chinese; a faithful English transcription is included in the supplementary material, and Table 15 maps the dataset’s option codes to the original wording. No information in this appendix was inferred from names, photos, or researcher impressions; undeclared fields are reported as such.

M.2. Aggregate profile

Table 14 summarizes the sample. Participants’ self-reported affiliations covered universities, public research institutes, and industry (32 academic, 4 industry among the 36 on record); participants reported their own gender (15 female, 21 male, 1 undisclosed) and age (M=24.7M{=}24.7, 𝑆𝐷=4.3\mathit{SD}{=}4.3, range 18–42).

Why field labels alone do not make this an “insider” sample.

A majority of participants (20/35) classified themselves into CS/AI disciplines, but the questionnaire deliberately separated disciplinary labels from agent-specific expertise, and the two diverge sharply. Most CS/AI-classified participants specialize in areas whose day-to-day work does not involve building or evaluating GUI agents, such as computer vision, embodied AI, computer architecture, NLP post-training, signal processing, and similar fields. Asked directly about professional background with agents, only 2/35 (5.7%) reported direct experience with computer-use/GUI agents, 5/35 reported agent (but not GUI-agent) backgrounds, 12/35 reported AI work unrelated to agents, and 16/35 reported no or only limited professional exposure to AI agents at all. Usage told the same story: 14/35 (40%) had never used a GUI agent or had tried one only once or twice before the study. The sample is therefore best characterized as technically literate but predominantly novice with respect to GUI agents, the population for which governance interfaces must work.

Participants’ existing AI usage was mainstream rather than specialist. The most-used products were conversational assistants (ChatGPT 31/35, DeepSeek 24, Claude 19, Gemini 18); coding assistants were common (Claude Code 13, GitHub Copilot 6, other coding agents 6, Cursor 3), while research-style tools (6), general-purpose agents (5), and any standalone computer-use/GUI-agent product (only 2) were rare. Reported purposes centered on research (27/35), coding (16), learning (15), and writing (10); delegating a multi-step task to an agent for autonomous completion was reported by only one participant. One additional participant reported essentially no AI use.

M.3. Instrument mapping

M.4. Per-participant roster

Table 16 lists every completer’s self-reported information. Field categories follow the questionnaire’s own option wording. Note in particular that the code math corresponded to “Mathematics / Statistics / Physics and other basic sciences,” so basic-science majors (e.g., physics) appear under that label; the parenthesized detail is the participant’s own free-text specialization, translated. Category codes follow the raw submission log; for one participant (P13) the compensation copy and the submission log differ on the category code (other vs. math), and we report the submission log.
